For six weeks Lena had trained Biscuit in Mrs. Farrow's backyard, an hour every evening after supper. Biscuit was Mrs. Farrow's dog, a young shepherd mix with one ear that stood up and one that flopped, and Mrs. Farrow, whose knees had grown too stiff for training, had asked Lena to handle him in the junior obedience class at the county fair.

By August he could heel, turn, and come on command. His best exercise was the long sit. Lena would tell him to stay, walk to the garden gate at the far end of the yard, turn, fold her arms, and wait. A full minute later he would still be sitting in the grass, watching her with his good ear up. When she wanted him, she let her arms drop to her sides and called his name, and he came at a gallop.

The ring at the fair was a rectangle of green carpet inside a low white fence. The judge, a tall man with a clipboard, explained the rules to the six handlers in a flat, practiced voice. For the long sit, handlers would cross the ring, turn, and stand with their arms hanging at their sides until he called time.

Biscuit heeled perfectly. He turned when she turned. He sat square at her left knee and looked up at her. Then Lena told him to stay, walked across the carpet, turned, and let her arms fall to her sides, as the judge had instructed.

Biscuit stood up, trotted to her with his tail going, and sat at her feet.

The judge wrote something on his clipboard. Two other dogs held their sits for the whole minute. Lena led Biscuit out of the ring with her face hot and a white ribbon for sixth place in her pocket.

Mrs. Farrow was waiting by the rail. On the walk to the car, Lena said that Biscuit had made a fool of her in front of everyone, and that he knew that exercise perfectly well.

"He did it exactly the way he always does it," Mrs. Farrow said. "What do you do with your hands when you want him to come?"

Lena opened her mouth to answer and then stopped walking.

The next evening she stood at the garden gate with her arms at her sides and said nothing at all. Biscuit looked at her hands, then at her face, and got up. She walked him back to his spot and tried again, and again, until he stayed. It took most of a week. Mrs. Farrow watched from the kitchen window and kept out of it.

On the last evening Lena stood at the gate for two full minutes with her arms hanging loose, and Biscuit sat in the grass and watched her, waiting for her to call his name.

item.passage:
Eleven at night, and the small airport
has shut its coffee stand and half its lights.
A belt of steel plates waits under a sign
that says Flight 418, and nothing moves.

Then a buzzer, a yellow lamp turning,
and the plates begin their slow oval
the way a dog circles before it lies down,
and the first bag noses through the rubber flaps.

It is black. So is the next, and the next,
black and the same size, zippered, wheeled,
as if one company had made the luggage
for everyone on earth and run out of colors.

But look how each one has been marked:
a green ribbon knotted on a handle,
a strip of silver tape, a luggage tag
shaped like a fish, a sticker of a lemon.

People lean in as the bags come past
and read the handles the way you scan a crowd
for one face, and then a hand shoots out,
and a man hauls his green ribbon off the belt.

My aunt is somewhere in the line behind the glass.
Her bag, she told me on the phone, is black.
"You'll know it," she said, and laughed,
and would say no more than that.

So I watch. The tape goes by, the fish goes by,
a stroller wrapped in plastic like a sandwich,
a box tied up with twine and somebody's name
printed on all four sides in marker.

The crowd thins. The belt keeps going.
Then out through the flaps comes a black bag
with a yellow tennis ball jammed on its handle,
fuzzy and chewed, the one her dog drops

at our feet on every visit until we throw it.
And here she comes through the sliding doors,
waving, already pointing at the belt,
and I have the bag off before she reaches me.

All night, around and around, the same black shapes,
and every one of them carrying
something small and silly that says mine,
so that whoever comes for it will know.

The week before my first job interview, the summer I was sixteen, I found out that I had no idea how to tie a necktie. I watched four videos in a row on my phone. In each one a calm man in a white shirt crossed the wide end over the narrow end, looped it around, and pulled it through, and in each one, by the time I had copied the first step, he was finished and smiling at the camera.

My father had worn a tie to the bank every working day for thirty-one years. When I asked him to show me, he stood facing me in the hallway, took the tie, and started. Then he stopped. He tried again, slowly, with his eyes on my collar, and got the wide end tangled under the narrow one. He frowned at it as though it belonged to someone else.

"Hold on," he said. "I've only ever done this on myself."

He walked me into the bathroom and stood behind me, looking into the mirror over my shoulder. He reached around me with both arms, the way he would have reached around his own neck, and took the two ends of the tie. In the mirror his hands moved quickly and without a pause: over, around, up through the loop, down through the front, and a tug at the knot. Under my chin sat a neat triangle, a little crooked.

"Again," I said. He pulled it loose and did it more slowly, saying each step out loud as his hands made it, as though he were hearing the names for the first time. Over. Around. Up. Down through. He had tied that knot more than seven thousand times, by my count later, and I doubt he had ever once put the steps into words.

Then he took my hands and set them on the two ends, and kept his own hands over mine, and we did it together, his hands steering, mine learning where to be. The first knot I made by myself, ten minutes later, was fat and lopsided. The fifth was good enough for an interview at a grocery store.

I got the job, stocking shelves, and wore the tie once, on the first day, when it turned out that nobody else did.

My father has been retired for two years and has given most of his ties away, but I wear one more often now. Every time, I stand in front of the mirror, and for a moment before my hands begin, I can feel the weight of his arms around my shoulders, and the knot comes out right. When my younger cousin asked me last spring to teach him, I started to explain, got lost after "around," and then laughed and walked around behind him.

He walked me into the bathroom and stood behind me, looking into the mirror over my shoulder. He reached around me with both arms, the way he would have reached around his own neck, and took the two ends of the tie. item.passage:
Most of the trees planted along city streets and in city parks are chosen for good behavior. They grow straight, put up with exhaust and salted sidewalks, and drop only leaves. Some are chosen precisely because they bear little or no fruit, since fruit falls, and fallen fruit is a mess that someone has to clean up.

I understand the reasoning, but I think cities have given up something valuable to avoid a few sticky sidewalks. A park with apple, pear, and plum trees in it offers what an ordinary park cannot: food, free for the taking, a short walk from people who may have little room or money for fresh fruit. It also offers a lesson that is hard to teach any other way. A child who has seen pears only in a store can watch one swell on a branch from June to September.

The objections are real, and they deserve an answer. The first is the mess. Fruit left on the ground rots, draws wasps, and stains the paths. The second is work. Fruit trees need pruning every winter and some protection from pests, which a parks department with a thin budget may be unable to give.

Both problems have the same answer, which is people. Cities that have planted public orchards have often done it with volunteer groups who prune in winter and harvest in late summer and fall, picking the fruit before it drops. What the volunteers and neighbors cannot eat, they can give to food banks. A tree that has been picked clean leaves little on the path to rot.

A third objection is that a few people will take everything. Perhaps some will. But the same complaint could be made about a public library, where a few borrowers keep books for months, and towns build libraries anyway. A shared thing is always open to a little misuse, and that has rarely been a good reason to have none of it.

It would be foolish to replace every street tree with an apple tree. Fruit trees belong where people gather and linger: parks, schoolyards, the edges of community gardens. A modest start, a dozen trees in one park and one group willing to look after them, would show quickly whether the idea works in a given city.

Planting any tree is a bet on the future, since the person who plants it may wait years to see it full grown. Planting a tree whose fruit anyone may pick is a second bet, on the neighbors. I think most neighbors are worth that bet.

item.passage:
In the 1830s the cattle, pigs, and sheep of Brayton Hollow spent much of the summer wherever they liked. Fences were costly to build, so a farmer usually fenced his crops in and let his animals wander the roads and the common. The trouble came when a neighbor's pigs broke into a field of turnips, or a stray heifer spent the night in someone's corn.

The town's answer, like that of many New England towns, was a pound: a square pen with stone walls about six feet high and a single wooden gate with a lock. Anyone who found a stray animal on his land could drive it to the pound. The pound keeper, chosen each spring at town meeting, fed and watered it and let it go only when its owner paid a fee of twenty-five cents a head, plus the cost of its feed.

For years the pound at Brayton Hollow stood mostly empty. The keeper was usually an older farmer with no wish to quarrel with his neighbors, and a man who drove a neighbor's cow to the pound could expect a cold reception at church for a month. Strays were simply driven home, with complaints, and the complaints piled up.

In the spring of 1841 the town meeting chose a new keeper, Abel Strand, a blacksmith who had come to the Hollow only three years earlier and was related to no one there. Some voters later admitted that they had chosen him partly as a joke. If so, it was the best joke the town ever played on itself.

Strand took the job exactly as it was written. Within his first week he had six pigs and two cows behind the stone walls, and one of the cows belonged to Josiah Merrow, the selectman who had written the town's rules for the pound eleven years before. Merrow came to the gate the next morning and asked for his cow. Strand showed him the rules, in Merrow's own handwriting, and named the fee.

What happened next was talked about in the Hollow for decades. Merrow read the page, counted out twenty-five cents and the price of a day's hay, and led his cow home. That Sunday he stood up after the service and said that a rule which bent for the man who wrote it was hardly a rule at all.

The effect was quick. By July, farmers who had let their pigs roam for years were mending their pens, and the complaints recorded at town meeting fell from thirty-one the year before to four. The pound was seldom full again. Its walls had done less than the knowledge that the keeper would use them.

Strand was chosen keeper every spring for the next nineteen years. The stone walls of the pound still stand at the corner of Merrow Road, though the gate rotted away long ago and the pen is full of young birches.
